case_title: Chotkau v. State of Uttar Pradesh
accused_socioeconomic_status: Poor; could not afford a lawyer at the Sessions Court stage and was provided an amicus advocate.
evidence_type: Circumstantial (last seen theory based on eyewitness testimony of PWs 1 to 3); post-mortem and unexhibited medical/forensic documents
aggravating_circumstances: Victim was a six-year-old girl; the offences of rape and murder were described by the Court as a shocking case; the lower courts held it one of the rarest of rare cases.
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under IPC ss.302 and 376 on circumstantial evidence; sentenced to death.
high_court_outcome: Death reference and accused's appeal dismissed; conviction and death sentence confirmed.
neutral_facts: A six-year-old girl, the niece of the accused, was reported to have been taken by the accused in the afternoon under the pretext of showing dance and song performances at a festival. When she did not return home, a search was conducted. The accused was not found at his house, and the girl's body was found in a sugarcane field on the southern side of the village. A villager who took part in the search said he saw the accused leaving the sugarcane field about half an hour later. Two other villagers said they saw the accused taking the girl towards the field. According to the prosecution, the first informant lodged a written complaint at the police station at about 8:10 p.m. the same day, and a head constable registered the FIR. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem prepared vaginal smears, but no positive finding was recorded in the evidence. Salwar worn by the victim was sent for forensic examination, but no forensic report was obtained. The accused was not medically examined. The prosecution relied on the last seen circumstances and on the accused's failure to explain what happened to the girl.
physical_harm: Death of a six-year-old girl; alleged rape
key_evidence_accepted: None of the eyewitness evidence of PWs 1 to 3 was accepted as trustworthy; the Court relied on the absence of medical examination and the unexplained FIR delay to find the case unproven.
witness_credibility: PWs 1 to 3 found completely untrustworthy because of serious mutual and other contradictions on how the FIR was lodged, where the body was first seen and taken, the place, date and time of inquest, and the clothes on the body. The Sessions Court and High Court wrongly treated these as minor.
post_offence_conduct: Prosecution case relied on the appellant being absconding when the body was found; the Supreme Court did not accept the evidence supporting this.
trial_duration: offence: 08.03.2012; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 18.04.2016; Supreme Court: 28.09.2022
legal_representation: Appellant: S. Nagamuthu, Senior Advocate, with others (including Ms. Shivani Misra). State: Ardhendumauli Kumar Prasad, Additional Advocate General, with others.
investigation_status: FIR registered on 08.03.2012 at Ikauna police station; post-mortem conducted; final report submitted to court; trial held.
procedural_irregularity: Five-day delay in forwarding FIR to the CJM (received 13.03.2012); no record of who took the FIR to court; no medical examination of the accused; forensic report on the salwar not obtained; unexhibited vaginal smear memo and report; contradictory inquest and body-handling evidence.
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.302 and 376 IPC, death sentence. High Court: confirmed conviction and death sentence. Supreme Court: appeals allowed, conviction and sentence set aside.
prosecution_argument: PWs 1 to 3 had no reason to implicate the accused; their evidence was found cogent and trustworthy by two courts; the FIR delay did not vitiate the trial or prejudice the accused; the forensic/medical evidence is not always mandatory.
defence_argument: PWs 1 to 3 untrustworthy; unexplained five-day delay in forwarding FIR; serious contradictions on the body and inquest; last seen evidence insufficient; material witnesses not examined; medical/forensic evidence not produced; s.313 questioning defective; false implication at the instance of a powerful local person.
legal_principle_applied: Panchsheel test for circumstantial evidence; trustworthiness of ocular evidence; word 'forthwith' in s.157(1) CrPC read in the facts of each case, with delay fatal where ocular evidence is unreliable; failure to medically examine the accused under s.53A is fatal where the victim is dead and the case is circumstantial.
precedent_relied_upon: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116; Meharaj Singh v. State of U.P (1994) 5 SCC 188; Bhajan Singh v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 421; Brahm Swaroop v. State of U.P (2011) 6 SCC 288; Balram Singh v. State of Punjab (2003) 11 SCC 286; State of Rajasthan v. Daud Khan (2016) 2 SCC 607; Jafarudheen v. State of Kerala (2022 SCC OnLine SC 495); Krishan Kumar Malik v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 130; Rajendra Pralhadrao Wasnik v. State of Maharashtra (2019) 12 SCC 460
other_sentence_order: Appellant to be released forthwith if not wanted in connection with any other case.
